newsitem.title: JAPAN: WTO rules Japan liquor taxes unfair - Japan sources.
newsitem.headline: WTO rules Japan liquor taxes unfair - Japan sources.

text.p: A World Trade Organisation (WTO) panel has decided that Japan's taxes on domestic spirits breach its rules, upholding an earlier ruling that the taxes are unfair, Japanese government sources said on Thursday.
The sources did not comment on whether Japan would change its taxation system after the international trade body formally issues its final ruling on the way Japan taxes local and imported spirits.
But Finance Ministry officials have said in recent months that if the WTO found against Japan, the country's liquor taxes may need to be revised.

The European Union has said that Japan taxes imported spirits at rates more than six times those imposed on popular domestic products called shochu. Tokyo has argued that shochu -- a potent, colourless liquor made from barley -- is basically a beverage for poorer people, while whiskey and other imported spirits are drunk by more affluent consumers.
A 700 millilitre bottle of imported whiskey retails for around 5,000 yen ($45) or more in Japan, while a bottle of shochu of about the same size costs around 850 yen ($7).
Meanwhile, industry analysts said Japan's liquor industry was not likely to suffer much from the WTO action.
"The situation would not change the structure of domestic demand, as shochu is still the cheapest alcohol in the country," said Shuichi Shibanuma, industry analyst at Merrill Lynch.

In July, the WTO said in its initial finding that Japan's system of liquor taxes treated imported spirits such as whiskey and brandy unfairly, to the advantage of domestic products. The WTO panel has been considering Japan's appeal against the initial ruling.
Shibanuma said that he did not expect the WTO's final ruling to have much of a negative impact on Japanese manufacturers of domestic spirits.
The only possible move that could change the trend of domestic demand is a cut in taxes on whiskey, but this is not likely to happen, he added.
Japan is not expected to slash taxes on imported spirits due to the country's mounting debts, probably opting instead to increase shochu taxes.
Masaaki Yamaguchi, an analyst at Nomura Research Institute, said a smaller gap between taxes on imported and domestic spirits was not likely to boost consumption of whiskey.
On the Tokyo Stock Exchange on Thursday, shares of top shochu maker Takara Shuzo Co Ltd fell on the reported WTO ruling, slipping 70 yen ($0.63) to close at 1,050 yen ($9).
Nomura's Yamaguchi said Takara Shuzo's shares had been somewhat overbought in the first place, so the shares still had scope for further declines.
